name: Toe Hold from 50-50 Guard
summary: The toe hold from 50-50 guard is a rotational ankle and foot lock that uses a figure-four grip on the toes and ball of the foot to twist the ankle, punishing opponents who hide their heel from heel hooks.
description: Master the toe hold from 50-50 guard in BJJ. Learn figure-four grip mechanics, rotational finishing details, and key defensive counters for this leg lock.
overview:
The toe hold from 50-50 guard exploits the unique foot accessibility created by this symmetrical leg entanglement. While most 50-50 attacks target the heel through heel hooks, the toe hold offers a devastating alternative that bypasses standard heel-hiding defenses. The attacker secures a figure-four grip on the opponent's foot, cupping the toes and ball of the foot with one hand while threading the opposite arm behind the ankle to complete the lock. Controlled rotational pressure through hip extension and wrist torque attacks the ankle ligaments, metatarsal joints, and midfoot structures simultaneously.

Strategically, the toe hold from 50-50 functions as a critical secondary weapon in the leg lock chain. Opponents who become skilled at tucking their heel to prevent heel hooks often inadvertently expose their foot for toe hold entries. This makes the toe hold an essential complement to heel hook attacks — when your opponent hides the heel, the toes and ball of the foot remain accessible. The 50-50 entanglement provides natural leg control that prevents the opponent from simply pulling their foot free, while the top position grants the hip extension needed to generate finishing pressure.

In competition, the toe hold from 50-50 has gained prominence as athletes develop more sophisticated heel hook defenses. The IBJJF restricts toe holds to brown and black belt divisions, reflecting the technique's injury potential. Under rulesets that permit the technique, it creates a genuine dilemma for defenders: protect the heel and expose the foot, or protect the foot and expose the heel. This forced choice between two dangers makes the toe hold from 50-50 a high-percentage finishing option for practitioners who invest in proper grip mechanics and controlled pressure application.

injury_risks.injury: Ankle ligament tears (lateral and medial collateral ligaments)
injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks with potential for chronic instability

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW - 5-7 seconds minimum from initial grip to any pressure. The toe hold attacks multiple small joints simultaneously and can cause damage before pain registers. Never apply sudden rotational force in training.
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on partner or mat (multiple taps)
Physical foot tap with free leg
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure on the foot
Allow opponent's foot to return to neutral position naturally
Maintain light contact until opponent signals they are okay
Check with training partner before continuing
training_restrictions: Never apply sudden rotational force — all pressure must be gradual and controlled
Never grip individual toes — always grip across multiple toes and ball of foot
Never combine toe hold pressure with explosive hip extension
Always allow clear tap access for both of your partner's hands
Stop immediately at any sign of discomfort or unusual popping
IBJJF legal only at brown and black belt — verify ruleset before competition use

variations_and_setups.description: Classic grip where the attacking hand cups across the toes and ball of the foot while the opposite arm threads behind the Achilles to complete the figure-four. Pressure is generated by pulling the foot toward your chest while extending your hips away from the opponent.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Default entry when opponent's foot is accessible and you have a clear path to thread the figure-four grip behind the ankle

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Heel hook feint to toe hold
variations_and_setups.description: Begin attacking the heel hook to force your opponent to hide their heel by tucking it inward. As they rotate the knee to protect the heel, their foot extends and the toes become accessible for the toe hold grip. The transition happens in the moment between their heel defense and repositioning.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents with strong heel hook defense who consistently hide the heel, creating a forced choice between heel exposure and foot exposure

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of attacking the inside foot trapped in the entanglement, target the opponent's outside foot that may be posted or free. Requires releasing one leg from the 50-50 to access the outside foot, then securing the figure-four from a modified angle with your body perpendicular to the opponent.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the inside foot is well defended but the opponent's outside foot is posted on the mat or accessible due to poor leg positioning

attacker.name: from 50-50 Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the toe hold from 50-50 guard. Step-by-step execution, grip details, common counters, and training progressions for BJJ leg lock finishing.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the toe hold from 50-50 guard requires precise figure-four grip placement and controlled rotational pressure. The 50-50 entanglement naturally controls your opponent's leg, allowing you to focus on grip mechanics and finishing details. The key attacking advantage is that this submission directly punishes opponents who hide their heel to defend heel hooks — when the heel disappears, the foot becomes your primary target. Success depends on securing the grip before your opponent can retract their foot, maintaining knee control through the entanglement to prevent spinning escapes, and applying slow, methodical pressure that gives your opponent time to recognize the danger and tap safely. The grip must encompass the toes and ball of the foot as a unit, never isolating individual toes, and the figure-four behind the ankle creates a mechanical system where hip extension translates directly into rotational force on the ankle joint.
key_principles: Figure-four grip integrity: the cupping hand controls toes and ball of foot as a single unit while the threading arm completes the lock behind the Achilles tendon
Rotational pressure through hip extension, not arm strength — your hips generate the torque while your arms maintain grip alignment
Knee control through the 50-50 entanglement prevents the opponent from spinning to relieve rotational pressure on the ankle
Attack timing exploits heel hook defense — initiate the toe hold grip when your opponent tucks their heel inward
Gradual pressure application with constant communication — this submission can damage structures before pain fully registers
Maintain inside leg position throughout the attack to prevent the opponent from collapsing the entanglement and escaping
setup_requirements: Established 50-50 entanglement with your inside leg maintaining control across the opponent's hip line
Top position with hip pressure preventing the opponent from sitting up to contest grips
Opponent's foot accessible — toes and ball of foot not tucked behind your body or hidden under their opposite leg
At least one hand free to initiate the figure-four grip while maintaining leg entanglement control
Opponent's knee controlled by the entanglement to prevent spinning out during grip establishment

execution_steps.action: Identify foot position and create access
execution_steps.description: From 50-50 top position, assess the opponent's foot position within the entanglement. If their heel is exposed, threaten the heel hook first to force them to tuck the heel inward, which extends the foot and exposes the toes. Maintain hip pressure throughout to prevent them from sitting up.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds for assessment and heel hook feint

execution_steps.action: Secure initial grip on toes and ball of foot
execution_steps.description: With your primary hand (typically the hand on the same side as the targeted foot), cup across the opponent's toes and ball of foot. Your fingers wrap over the top of the toes while your palm presses against the ball of the foot. Grip the foot as a single unit — never isolate individual toes.

execution_steps.action: Thread the figure-four arm behind the ankle
execution_steps.description: Pass your opposite arm behind the opponent's Achilles tendon and ankle, threading it through until your hand can grip your own wrist or forearm to complete the figure-four configuration. The threading arm should sit snugly in the groove behind the ankle bone, not on the calf or lower shin.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds for threading and grip completion

execution_steps.action: Lock the figure-four and consolidate control
execution_steps.description: Secure the figure-four by gripping your own wrist with the threading hand (gable grip or wrist-to-wrist). Pull the foot tight against your chest so there is no slack in the grip configuration. Your elbows should be pinched together, creating a compact structure that resists grip breaks.

Position your hips so that hip extension will drive the foot into inward rotation (twisting the toes toward the opponent's centerline/midline, the pinky toe moving toward their opposite hip). Your hips should be slightly offset toward the inside of the trapped leg. Tighten your leg entanglement to prevent the opponent from spinning their knee to relieve the rotational angle.

Slowly extend your hips away from the opponent while simultaneously pulling the foot toward your chest with the figure-four grip. This creates rotational torque on the ankle joint. Apply pressure gradually over 5-7 seconds minimum, increasing incrementally. Monitor your opponent's reaction and stop immediately upon any tap signal. The finish comes from the combined force of hip extension and grip rotation, not from jerking or explosive movement.
execution_steps.timing: 5-7 seconds minimum for controlled pressure application

execution_steps.description: As the opponent feels the pressure, they will attempt to rotate, grip fight, or bridge to relieve torque. Maintain your grip integrity by keeping elbows pinched and the foot pressed against your chest. Follow their body movement with your hips to preserve the rotational angle. If they begin to spin their body, tighten your leg entanglement to anchor their knee in place while continuing steady pressure.

common_counters.counter: Boot retraction — opponent pulls foot back toward their body to deny grip access
common_counters.your_response: Threaten heel hook first to force them to choose between heel exposure and foot exposure. When they tuck the heel, the foot extends and becomes accessible. Alternatively, use your outside hand to trap their ankle before they can fully retract.

common_counters.counter: Spinning out — opponent rotates their entire body to align their knee with the rotational force, removing torque
common_counters.your_response: Tighten your leg entanglement before applying rotational pressure to anchor their knee. If they begin spinning, follow their rotation with your hips and consider transitioning to a heel hook on the now-exposed heel as they turn.

common_counters.counter: Figure-four grip strip — opponent uses both hands to break the figure-four configuration
common_counters.your_response: Keep elbows pinched tight and the foot pressed firmly against your chest to maximize grip strength. If they commit both hands to grip fighting, they abandon their own leg defense — transition to heel hook or kneebar while their hands are occupied.

common_counters.counter: Counter leg entanglement — opponent attacks your exposed leg with their own submission while you focus on the toe hold
common_counters.your_response: Maintain awareness of your own leg exposure throughout the attack. If you feel them securing a grip on your heel or foot, assess whether you can finish faster or whether you need to abandon the toe hold and address your own defense first.

common_errors.error: Gripping individual toes instead of cupping across the entire ball of the foot
common_errors.consequence: Individual toe grips create localized force that can fracture or dislocate single toes before the opponent feels sufficient pain to tap, causing unnecessary injury
common_errors.correction: Always cup across all toes and the ball of the foot as a single unit. Your palm should cover the metatarsal heads while your fingers wrap over the top of the toes together

common_errors.error: Applying explosive or jerking rotational force instead of gradual pressure
common_errors.consequence: Sudden force can tear ankle ligaments or rupture the plantar fascia before the opponent has time to tap, potentially causing serious injury
common_errors.correction: Apply pressure over a minimum of 5-7 seconds from initial engagement to full torque. Increase incrementally and monitor opponent's reaction at each stage

common_errors.error: Threading the figure-four arm too high on the calf instead of behind the ankle
common_errors.consequence: A high grip reduces mechanical advantage and allows the opponent to slip their foot free by dorsiflexing, negating the entire submission
common_errors.correction: Thread the arm so it sits directly behind the ankle bone in the natural groove between the Achilles tendon and the joint. The arm should contact bone, not muscle

common_errors.error: Losing inside leg control during the grip setup phase
common_errors.consequence: Without inside leg control through the entanglement, the opponent can freely spin to relieve rotational pressure or extract their leg entirely
common_errors.correction: Establish and verify inside leg control before beginning the grip sequence. If inside position is compromised during setup, re-establish it before continuing the attack

common_errors.error: Relying on arm strength for the finish instead of hip extension
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly and cannot generate sufficient sustained torque. The submission stalls and the opponent has time to mount a defense
common_errors.correction: Use hip extension as the primary force generator. Your arms maintain grip alignment while your hips drive away from the opponent, creating rotational torque through the lever system

common_errors.error: Attacking the toe hold without first threatening the heel hook
common_errors.consequence: Without the heel hook threat, the opponent has no reason to hide their heel and can maintain a neutral foot position that makes both the toe hold and heel hook harder to secure
common_errors.correction: Always establish the heel hook threat first. The toe hold becomes highest percentage when the opponent actively defends the heel hook by tucking their heel, which extends and exposes the foot

training_progressions.description: Practice the figure-four grip on a compliant partner's foot without any resistance. Focus on cupping the toes and ball of foot correctly, threading the arm behind the ankle in the proper groove, and completing the figure-four with elbows pinched. Repeat 20-30 times per side until the grip sequence is automatic.

With the figure-four secured on a compliant partner, practice applying very slow rotational pressure through hip extension. Partner provides verbal feedback on pressure levels. Goal is to develop sensitivity for how much force produces each level of discomfort. Never exceed 30% effort in this phase.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Entry from 50-50 with light resistance
training_progressions.focus: Full sequence from 50-50 entry to grip to controlled finish
training_progressions.description: Start in 50-50 top position. Partner provides 30-50% resistance on the grip entry but cooperates once the figure-four is secured. Practice the heel hook feint to toe hold transition. Focus on maintaining inside leg control throughout the sequence.

Positional rounds starting in 50-50 with full resistance. Attacker works the heel hook to toe hold chain while defender uses all available counters. Reset if either person escapes or submits. Focus on recognizing when the toe hold is available versus when to stay with heel hook attacks.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the toe hold from 50-50 guard primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The toe hold primarily attacks the ankle ligaments (lateral and medial collateral), the metatarsal joints connecting the toes to the midfoot, the plantar fascia along the bottom of the foot, and the Lisfranc joint complex in the midfoot. The rotational force is distributed across multiple small structures simultaneously, which is why the technique can cause damage before significant pain registers — making controlled application essential.

flashcards.question: Why should you threaten the heel hook before attacking the toe hold from 50-50?
flashcards.answer: Threatening the heel hook forces the opponent into a defensive choice. When they tuck their heel inward to hide it from the heel hook, their foot naturally extends and the toes and ball of the foot become accessible for the toe hold grip. Without this threat, the opponent can maintain a neutral foot position that makes both attacks harder to secure. The heel hook feint creates the dilemma that makes the toe hold high-percentage.

flashcards.question: What is the correct hand position for the figure-four grip on the foot?
flashcards.answer: The primary hand cups across all toes and the ball of the foot as a single unit, with the palm pressing against the metatarsal heads and fingers wrapping over the tops of the toes. The opposite arm threads behind the ankle in the groove between the Achilles tendon and the ankle bone, then grips the wrist of the cupping hand to complete the figure-four. Elbows stay pinched together with the foot pressed against your chest.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts spinning their body to relieve rotational pressure — what adjustment prevents escape?
flashcards.answer: Tighten your leg entanglement by squeezing your legs together to anchor their knee in place, preventing further rotation. Follow their rotational movement with your own hips to maintain the angle of torque. If they continue spinning despite your leg control, consider transitioning to a heel hook on the heel that becomes exposed as they rotate away from the toe hold.

flashcards.question: What is the minimum time you should take to apply full rotational pressure when finishing the toe hold in training?
flashcards.answer: A minimum of 5-7 seconds from initial grip engagement to full rotational pressure. The toe hold attacks multiple small joints and ligaments simultaneously, and structural damage can occur before the defender feels adequate pain to recognize the danger. Gradual application over several seconds gives the opponent time to assess the threat and tap before injury occurs. In training, err on the side of even slower application.

flashcards.question: How does the 50-50 entanglement contribute to the toe hold finish compared to other positions?
flashcards.answer: The 50-50 entanglement provides built-in knee control that prevents the opponent from freely spinning to relieve rotational pressure on the ankle. The symmetrical leg configuration also means the opponent's foot is naturally positioned within reach rather than being retracted behind their body. Additionally, the top position in 50-50 provides the hip extension angle needed to generate finishing torque through the figure-four system.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the toe hold is close to the breaking point?
flashcards.answer: Indicators include the opponent's foot beginning to rotate inward (medially) beyond its natural range, visible tension in the Achilles tendon and ankle structures, the opponent's body stiffening or bridging involuntarily, and audible distress or sharp intake of breath. At the first sign of any of these indicators in training, pause pressure and allow the opponent to tap rather than continuing to increase torque. The gap between discomfort and structural failure is very small with toe holds.

flashcards.question: Your opponent commits both hands to stripping your figure-four grip — what opportunity does this create?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent dedicates both hands to breaking your toe hold grip, they abandon all defensive control of their own legs and heel. This creates an immediate opportunity to release the toe hold and transition to a heel hook, since the heel they were previously protecting is now undefended. Alternatively, transition to a kneebar by releasing the foot and controlling above the knee. The opponent cannot simultaneously strip your grip and defend their heel.

defender.name: from 50-50 Guard Defender
defender.description: Defend the toe hold from 50-50 guard in BJJ. Recognition cues, escape techniques, grip defense strategies, and training drills to survive this dangerous leg lock.
defender.overview: Defending the toe hold from 50-50 guard requires early recognition of the figure-four grip setup and immediate action to prevent the lock from being fully secured. The 50-50 entanglement limits your mobility and makes prevention far more effective than late-stage escapes once the grip is locked. Your primary defensive tools are grip fighting to prevent the figure-four configuration, foot retraction to deny access to your toes, and rotational alignment of your knee to reduce torque on the ankle. Understanding when to tap is particularly critical with the toe hold — unlike many submissions where pain provides a clear warning, the toe hold attacks multiple small structures simultaneously and can cause ligament damage before intense pain fully registers. Early recognition and proactive grip defense are your strongest weapons against this submission.
key_principles: Prevent the grip before it locks — breaking the figure-four configuration before it is completed requires far less effort than escaping after it is secure
Foot retraction is your first line of defense: pull your toes back toward your shin (dorsiflexion) and tuck the foot behind your opposite leg when possible
Align your knee with the rotational force by turning your knee inward toward the direction the attacker is twisting, which reduces the effective torque on the ankle
Monitor both heel and foot exposure simultaneously — hiding the heel from heel hooks can expose the foot for toe holds and vice versa
Tap early with toe holds — structural damage can occur before pain provides adequate warning, making the standard threshold of tapping at pain onset too late for safety
Counter-attack when the attacker commits to the grip — their focus on the toe hold often exposes their own heel for counter submissions
recognition_cues: Attacker's hand reaches for your toes or ball of your foot with a cupping motion instead of targeting your heel
Attacker's opposite arm begins threading behind your ankle or Achilles tendon to establish the figure-four
Attacker feints a heel hook then immediately redirects to your foot as you hide your heel
Attacker's elbows begin pinching together as they consolidate the figure-four grip against your foot and chest
You feel your foot being pulled toward the attacker's chest with rotational intent rather than the straight pull of an ankle lock

defensive_options.action: Aggressive grip fighting to prevent figure-four completion
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you recognize the attacker reaching for your toes or threading behind your ankle — before the figure-four locks
defensive_options.if_successful: Returns to neutral 50-50 position where you can address leg entanglement and work your own attacks or escapes
defensive_options.risk: Committing both hands to grip fighting leaves your heel temporarily undefended for heel hook transitions

defensive_options.action: Foot retraction and dorsiflexion — pull toes toward shin and tuck foot behind opposite leg
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing toe hold intent, especially after hiding your heel from a heel hook threat
defensive_options.if_successful: Denies the attacker access to the toes and ball of foot needed for the submission grip, forcing them to abandon or change attacks
defensive_options.risk: Pulling the foot back may momentarily expose the heel if the attacker transitions quickly to heel hook

defensive_options.action: Knee rotation and body spin to align with rotational force
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four grip is already secured and you cannot break it — rotate your knee and body in the direction the attacker is twisting
defensive_options.if_successful: Reduces effective rotational torque on the ankle by aligning the joint with the applied force, buying time to work grip breaks
defensive_options.risk: Spinning may compromise your leg entanglement position and give the attacker better control angles

defensive_options.action: Counter leg attack — attack the attacker's exposed heel or foot while they focus on your toe hold
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits both arms to the figure-four, leaving their own legs undefended
defensive_options.if_successful: Forces the attacker to release the toe hold to address their own defense, creating a scramble that can lead to guard recovery
defensive_options.risk: Racing to submit while being submitted is extremely dangerous — only attempt if you are confident you can force the release before your ankle is compromised

escape_paths: Strip the figure-four grip using two-on-one hand fighting on the cupping hand, then immediately retract foot and re-establish heel defense
Spin your body in the direction of the rotational force to nullify torque while working grip breaks, then extract your leg from the entanglement
Counter-attack with your own heel hook or toe hold on the attacker's exposed leg to force them to release and defend

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully strip the figure-four grip through aggressive hand fighting before the attacker can apply significant rotational pressure, then use the scramble to establish top position in the 50-50 entanglement
Counter-attack the attacker's exposed leg to force a release, then use the scramble to extract your legs from the entanglement and pull the attacker into your closed guard

common_errors.error: Waiting until pain registers before beginning defensive action
common_errors.consequence: The toe hold can damage ankle ligaments and midfoot structures before significant pain develops, meaning waiting for pain as a tap signal can result in structural injury
common_errors.correction: Begin defensive action as soon as you recognize the grip setup. If the figure-four is fully locked and rotational pressure has begun, tap early rather than testing your pain threshold

common_errors.error: Hiding the heel so aggressively that the foot becomes fully exposed
common_errors.consequence: Tucking the heel inward to defend against heel hooks extends the foot forward, giving the attacker direct access to the toes and ball of the foot for the toe hold
common_errors.correction: When hiding the heel, simultaneously retract the foot by pulling toes toward your shin and tucking the entire foot behind your opposite leg, not just rotating the heel inward

common_errors.error: Attempting to straighten the leg to pull the foot away from the figure-four grip
common_errors.consequence: Straightening the leg while the figure-four is locked increases the lever arm and amplifies rotational force on the ankle, accelerating the submission rather than escaping it
common_errors.correction: Keep the knee bent and focus on rotational alignment and grip stripping rather than leg extension. Work the grip with your hands while keeping the knee flexed to minimize the lever arm

common_errors.error: Ignoring own leg defense while racing to counter-attack the attacker's legs
common_errors.consequence: Mutual leg lock exchanges with toe holds are extremely dangerous because both submissions can cause damage before the tap. You risk serious ankle injury while attempting to apply your own submission
common_errors.correction: Only counter-attack if you are confident you can force the attacker to release before your ankle is compromised. When in doubt, focus entirely on grip defense and extraction rather than counter-offense

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a toe hold is being set up from 50-50 rather than a heel hook?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cue is the attacker's hand targeting your toes and ball of the foot with a cupping motion rather than reaching for the heel. Additionally, you will feel the attacker's opposite arm threading behind your ankle to establish the figure-four configuration. If you have been hiding your heel from a heel hook threat, the transition to toe hold often occurs immediately after the attacker redirects from the heel to the exposed foot.

flashcards.question: Why is it critical to tap earlier to a toe hold than to many other submissions?
flashcards.answer: The toe hold simultaneously attacks multiple small joints and ligaments in the foot, ankle, and midfoot. Unlike submissions that primarily create a single point of intense pain (such as the armbar at the elbow), the toe hold distributes force across many structures. This means ligament tears and joint damage can occur before pain provides adequate warning. Tap at the first sign of significant rotational pressure rather than waiting for sharp pain.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available when the figure-four grip is already locked?
flashcards.answer: Once the figure-four is locked, your options narrow significantly. Rotate your knee and body in the direction the attacker is twisting to reduce effective torque on the ankle. Use two-on-one grip fighting to strip the cupping hand from your toes. If you cannot break the grip and pressure is increasing, tap immediately rather than attempting a desperate escape that could cause injury. Counter-attacking is risky at this stage but forcing a scramble may create an opening.

flashcards.question: How should you balance heel defense and foot defense in 50-50 against an opponent who chains heel hooks and toe holds?
flashcards.answer: The key is retracting the entire foot rather than just rotating one structure. When hiding the heel, simultaneously pull the toes toward the shin through dorsiflexion and tuck the whole foot behind your opposite leg. This protects both heel and toes at the same time. Maintain constant grip control on the attacker's hands to prevent them from accessing either target. If forced to choose, prioritize whichever attack the opponent is currently threatening and be ready to transition your defense instantly when they switch.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying toe hold setups versus heel hook setups
training_progressions.description: Partner alternates between heel hook and toe hold grip entries from 50-50 at half speed. Defender calls out which attack is being initiated. Build pattern recognition for the cupping hand on toes versus the heel grip. No resistance needed — focus purely on visual and tactile recognition.

training_progressions.focus: Stopping the figure-four before it completes
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to establish the toe hold figure-four grip at 50% speed. Defender practices foot retraction, grip fighting to prevent the threading arm, and two-on-one grip breaks if the figure-four begins to form. Reset each time the grip is prevented or broken.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Late-stage defense and tapping awareness
training_progressions.focus: Surviving after the grip is locked and knowing when to tap
training_progressions.description: Partner secures the figure-four grip and applies very slow, controlled pressure. Defender practices knee rotation, body spinning, and grip stripping under pressure. Emphasis on recognizing the point where defense has failed and tapping cleanly before injury. Partner must apply pressure extremely slowly in this phase.

training_progressions.focus: Integrating all defensive tools against live toe hold and heel hook chains
training_progressions.description: Full positional sparring from 50-50 bottom against an attacker who chains heel hooks and toe holds. Defender uses all recognition, prevention, and escape tools. Track success rate of preventing the grip versus needing to defend the locked submission. Goal is preventing 80% of grip establishments.
